title: Phishing at 5 PM
summary: A last-minute Teams message from 'IT Support' asks for your token code. Can you avoid the trap?
briefing: It is 5 PM and you are wrapping up for the day while working from home. A Teams message pops up from someone claiming to be from IT Support: 'Your access will expire today. Please share your token code now to avoid account lockout.' The pressure is on. Investigate and escape safely.
scenario: Threat vector: Teams direct message impersonating IT Support. The request is to share an MFA token/OTP code under time pressure to 'avoid lockout'. Red flags: unsolicited contact, request for credentials/token, manufactured urgency, external/guest account.
objectives: Recognise that IT will never ask for your token or password
Report the attempt through the correct channel

steps.prompt: The 'IT Support' contact insists you share your token code in the next few minutes or be locked out. What is your first move?
steps.clue: Genuine IT support never needs your token, password or OTP to help you.

choices.text: Share the token quickly so you don't get locked out
choices.feedback: Never share tokens or OTPs. This is exactly how accounts get compromised.

choices.text: Ignore the message and log off
choices.feedback: Ignoring it protects you, but the attacker will simply try the next colleague.

choices.text: Verify the sender's identity and report the suspicious activity
choices.feedback: Correct. Verify independently and report — you protect yourself and others.

choices.text: Forward the message to a teammate to ask what to do
choices.feedback: Forwarding can spread the lure and leak details. Report it instead.

steps.prompt: You take a closer look at the sender before doing anything. Which detail is the strongest evidence this is an attack?
steps.clue: Focus on WHO is really messaging you and WHAT they are asking for.

choices.text: They used my first name, so it feels personal and genuine
choices.feedback: Your name is easy to find and is not proof of identity.

choices.text: The account is an external/guest user, and IT is asking for my token code
choices.feedback: Correct. An external account asking for credentials is a decisive red flag.

choices.text: The message has no spelling mistakes, so it must be real
choices.feedback: Modern phishing is well written. Good grammar proves nothing.

choices.text: It is urgent, so I should act faster to be safe
choices.feedback: Urgency is the manipulation — it is a reason to slow down, not speed up.

steps.prompt: You are confident this is a phishing attempt. How do you resolve it correctly?
steps.clue: Use the official reporting path; do not engage the attacker.

choices.text: Reply and ask them to prove they are really from IT
choices.feedback: Engaging confirms your account is active and invites more attempts.

choices.text: Report the message via the official 'Report Phishing' channel and block the sender
choices.feedback: Correct. Reporting lets Security protect the whole organisation.

choices.text: Delete it quietly and tell no one
choices.feedback: Silent deletion means colleagues stay exposed to the same attack.

choices.text: Share the token but change it right after
choices.feedback: Once shared, the attacker can act instantly. The damage is done.

learningPoints: IT will never ask for your password, token or OTP — anyone who does is an attacker.
Unsolicited contact + urgency + a request for credentials is a classic phishing pattern.
Report suspicious messages through the official channel and block the sender.
Verifying independently, via a known contact, breaks the attack.

sender.finding: The Teams account is an external/guest user, not an internal colleague
sender.meaning: IT Support requests never come from external guest accounts.

request.finding: They are asking for your MFA token/OTP code
request.meaning: no legitimate process ever needs your token — this alone confirms an attack.

urgency.finding: You are told to act 'in the next few minutes' to avoid lockout
urgency.meaning: manufactured urgency is designed to stop you thinking.

channel.finding: IT is reaching out via unsolicited DM rather than the official Service Desk
channel.meaning: verify through the known Service Desk channel instead.

title: Confidential File Leak
summary: A stressed colleague asks you to email a client data export to their personal address. Do you help?
briefing: A colleague messages you close to a deadline: 'Can you export the full client list and send it to my personal Gmail? I'll finish the analysis tonight at home — otherwise I'll get in trouble.' They are counting on you. What do you do?
scenario: Threat vector: internal request to exfiltrate confidential client data to a personal email account. The file contains names, account numbers and balances (Confidential / Personal data). Red flags: personal email destination, confidential client data, no approval, deadline pressure.
objectives: Recognise an unapproved external data transfer
Escalate to the right control owners

steps.prompt: Your colleague needs the client export sent to their personal email tonight. What do you do first?
steps.clue: Before moving any file, ask: what data is in it, and where is it going?

choices.text: Export and send it — they're on the team and it's urgent
choices.feedback: Sending confidential data to a personal account is a data leak, regardless of intent.

choices.text: Pause and check how the data is classified and where it's going
choices.feedback: Correct. Classification and destination determine whether this is allowed.

choices.text: Send just a 'small sample' to be helpful
choices.feedback: Even a sample of client records leaving managed systems is a breach.

choices.text: Upload it to a public file-sharing link instead
choices.feedback: Public links are worse — anyone with the URL can access confidential data.

steps.prompt: You inspect the file. Which fact makes this request unacceptable?
steps.clue: Look at the content of the file and the destination together.

choices.text: The file contains client names, account numbers and balances, and it's going to a personal Gmail
choices.feedback: Correct. Confidential/personal data must never leave managed systems for personal accounts.

choices.text: The file is quite large to email
choices.feedback: Size is not the issue — the confidentiality and destination are.

choices.text: It's after working hours
choices.feedback: The time of day doesn't change the data protection rules.

choices.text: Nothing — they'll delete it after using it
choices.feedback: A promise to delete does not make an unauthorised transfer acceptable.

steps.prompt: How do you handle this the right way?
steps.clue: Offer a safe alternative and involve the right people.

choices.text: Refuse politely, suggest doing the work inside approved systems, and flag it to your manager/DPO
choices.feedback: Correct. Protect the data, help the colleague safely, and escalate appropriately.

choices.text: Send it this once but warn them not to ask again
choices.feedback: A single unauthorised transfer is still a reportable data leak.

choices.text: Do nothing and hope they find another way
choices.feedback: Doing nothing risks the colleague leaking it via someone else.

choices.text: Password-protect the file and then email it to Gmail
choices.feedback: A password doesn't authorise sending confidential data to a personal account.

learningPoints: Confidential/personal client data must never be sent to personal email or public links.
Deadline pressure does not override data protection controls.
Offer a safe alternative: keep the work inside approved, managed systems.
Escalate suspected data leaks to your manager and Data Protection Officer.

request.finding: The export 'clients_full_export.xlsx' holds names, account numbers and balances
request.meaning: this is Confidential / Personal data under the classification standard.

channel.finding: The destination is a personal @gmail.com account
channel.meaning: moving confidential data outside managed systems is a reportable leak.

urgency.finding: The colleague says they'll 'get in trouble' unless it's sent now
urgency.meaning: pressure is being used to bypass controls.

title: Suspicious Vendor Request
summary: An existing vendor emails asking to change their bank details before the next payment run. Genuine or fraud?
briefing: An email arrives from a known vendor: 'Please update our bank account for the upcoming invoice — our old account is being closed. Payment is due tomorrow, so we need this changed today.' The signature and logo look right. Do you update the details?
scenario: Threat vector: Business Email Compromise (BEC). A supplier requests an urgent bank-account change before an invoice run. Red flags: changed bank details, reply-to domain mismatch, urgency, no independent verification.
objectives: Spot the signs of Business Email Compromise

steps.prompt: The vendor wants their bank details changed today for tomorrow's payment. What is your first action?
steps.clue: Any change to payment details should trigger a verification control.

choices.text: Update the details — the email looks legitimate
choices.feedback: Appearance is not verification. This is how BEC fraud succeeds.

choices.text: Independently verify the request using the vendor's known contact on file
choices.feedback: Correct. Call back on a trusted number — never the one in the email.

choices.text: Reply to the email to confirm the new account number
choices.feedback: You'd be confirming with the attacker, not the vendor.

choices.text: Make the change but keep a note in case it's wrong
choices.feedback: A note won't recover funds sent to a fraudulent account.

steps.prompt: You examine the email header. What is the clearest warning sign?
steps.clue: Compare the sender/reply-to address with the vendor's real domain.

choices.text: The reply-to address is a look-alike domain, different from the vendor on file
choices.feedback: Correct. A mismatched reply-to domain is a hallmark of BEC.

choices.text: The email has the vendor's logo, so it's genuine
choices.feedback: Logos are trivial to copy and mean nothing on their own.

choices.text: The invoice number looks normal
choices.feedback: A plausible invoice number doesn't verify a bank-detail change.

choices.text: It was sent during business hours
choices.feedback: Timing is not a control for payment changes.

steps.prompt: How do you correctly resolve the request?
steps.clue: Do not change details until verified; involve the right team.

choices.text: Hold the change, verify via the number on file, and escalate to Vendor Management
choices.feedback: Correct. Verified change control prevents payment fraud.

choices.text: Change it now and verify afterwards to avoid a late payment
choices.feedback: Once paid, the money is gone. Verify first, always.

choices.text: Ask the requester to email a scanned letter as proof
choices.feedback: Attackers can forge letters too — only a trusted call-back verifies.

choices.text: Ignore it; the vendor will chase if it's real
choices.feedback: Ignoring risks a genuine issue; the right step is verify-and-escalate.

learningPoints: Any request to change vendor bank details must be verified via a known, trusted contact.
A mismatched reply-to/look-alike domain is a classic Business Email Compromise sign.
Never verify using contact details supplied in the suspicious email itself.
Escalate payment-change requests to Vendor Management before acting.

sender.finding: The reply-to domain is a look-alike, not the vendor's registered domain
sender.meaning: this strongly indicates Business Email Compromise.

request.finding: They request an urgent bank-account change before the payment run

urgency.finding: They warn the payment will be late without immediate action
urgency.meaning: urgency is used to bypass the verification control.

title: AI Tool Misuse
summary: A teammate wants to paste client data and source code into a public AI chatbot to save time. Is that OK?
briefing: During a busy release, a teammate says: 'Let's just paste the client records and our service's source code into a public AI chatbot — it'll debug and summarise it in seconds.' It would genuinely save hours. What do you advise?
scenario: Threat vector: entering confidential/personal data and proprietary code into an unapproved public LLM. Red flags: confidential data in a public tool, provider data retention, no approval, sanctioned alternative exists.
objectives: Recognise confidential data must not enter unapproved AI tools
Redirect to the approved internal AI platform

steps.prompt: Your teammate is about to paste client records and code into a public AI chatbot. What do you say?
steps.clue: Think about where the data goes once it leaves the bank's systems.

choices.text: Go ahead — it's faster and everyone uses these tools
choices.feedback: Confidential data in a public tool is a confidentiality and data-protection breach.

choices.text: Stop — confidential data and proprietary code must not go into unapproved public tools
choices.feedback: Correct. Protect the data first; find a sanctioned way to get the benefit.

choices.text: Only paste the client data, not the code
choices.feedback: Client/personal data is exactly what must never be pasted into public tools.

choices.text: Paste it but ask the tool not to store it
choices.feedback: You can't rely on a public tool's promise; the data has already left.

steps.prompt: Why specifically is pasting into the public chatbot a problem?
steps.clue: Consider the provider's terms and what happens to your inputs.

choices.text: The provider may retain and train on the inputs, exposing confidential/personal data
choices.feedback: Correct. Loss of control over confidential data is the core risk.

choices.text: The AI might give a slightly wrong answer
choices.feedback: Accuracy matters, but the leak of confidential data is the critical risk here.

choices.text: It could be slow at peak times
choices.feedback: Performance is irrelevant to the data-protection breach.

choices.text: There's no problem if we're quick
choices.feedback: Speed doesn't reduce the confidentiality risk at all.

steps.clue: There is a sanctioned way to get AI help safely.

choices.text: Use the approved internal AI platform that keeps data inside the bank, and follow AI-usage guidance
choices.feedback: Correct. Get the productivity benefit through sanctioned, governed tooling.

choices.text: Anonymise names and paste the rest into the public tool
choices.feedback: Ad-hoc anonymisation is unreliable and code/context can still be sensitive.

choices.text: Ask a manager to approve using the public tool 'just this once'
choices.feedback: The right answer is the sanctioned platform, not an exception for a public tool.

choices.text: Skip AI entirely and do everything manually forever
choices.feedback: Not necessary — approved tools let you use AI safely.

learningPoints: Never enter confidential, personal or proprietary information into unapproved public AI tools.
Public tools may retain and train on your inputs — you lose control of the data.
Use the bank's approved internal AI platform to get the benefit safely.
Follow the Responsible AI and Acceptable Use guidance for any AI tooling.

request.finding: The plan is to paste client records and source code into a public LLM
request.meaning: confidential/personal data must never enter unapproved external tools.

channel.finding: The public tool's terms permit retaining and training on inputs
channel.meaning: this causes a loss of control and a confidentiality breach.

urgency.finding: The justification is purely to 'save hours' during a release
urgency.meaning: time pressure is not a reason to bypass data protection.

title: Client Data Handling
summary: A caller who fails identity checks demands their full account details 'because it's an emergency'. What now?
briefing: You take a call from someone claiming to be a client. They cannot answer two of the required security questions, but they insist: 'This is an emergency, just read me my account number and balance!' They are becoming aggressive. How do you respond?
scenario: Threat vector: social engineering over the phone to extract client account data after failed identity verification. Red flags: failed verification, emotional pressure, request for sensitive data.

steps.prompt: The caller failed identity verification but demands their account details. What do you do?
steps.clue: Disclosure depends entirely on verified identity — not on how urgent the caller sounds.

choices.text: Read out the details — they sound genuinely distressed
choices.feedback: Distress is not identity. Disclosing to an unverified caller is a data breach.

choices.text: Do not disclose anything and continue to follow the verification procedure
choices.feedback: Correct. No verification means no disclosure — full stop.

choices.text: Give partial details as a compromise
choices.feedback: Even partial disclosure to an unverified caller is a breach.

choices.text: Ask them to confirm the account number and then proceed
choices.feedback: Letting them supply the answer defeats the purpose of verification.

steps.prompt: The caller escalates and becomes aggressive. What is the right mindset?
steps.clue: Pressure and emotion are classic social-engineering levers.

choices.text: The pressure is a manipulation tactic; procedure protects both the client and me
choices.feedback: Correct. Stay calm and follow procedure regardless of pressure.

choices.text: Aggressive callers are usually genuine, so I should help faster
choices.feedback: Aggression is often used precisely to push staff into breaking rules.

choices.text: I should bend the rules to de-escalate
choices.feedback: Bending data-protection rules to calm someone is never acceptable.

choices.text: I should hang up immediately without explanation
choices.feedback: Better to remain professional, explain the process, and escalate.

steps.prompt: How do you resolve the call correctly?
steps.clue: Offer the compliant route and involve a supervisor if needed.

choices.text: Explain the verification requirement, offer the secure route to regain access, and escalate to a supervisor
choices.feedback: Correct. You protect the client's data and give them a legitimate path forward.

choices.text: Make an exception this once and note it afterwards
choices.feedback: A single exception is still a data breach.

choices.text: Transfer them randomly to get them off your line
choices.feedback: Dumping the call doesn't follow procedure or help the real client.

choices.text: Tell them to post their ID documents to the office
choices.feedback: That's not the approved secure verification route.

learningPoints: No identity verification means no disclosure of client data — without exception.
Emotional pressure and aggression are deliberate social-engineering tactics.
Offer the client a secure, approved route to regain access.
Escalate difficult cases to a supervisor rather than bending the rules.

request.finding: The caller cannot answer two required security questions
request.meaning: identity is not verified, so account data must not be disclosed.

urgency.finding: They claim an emergency and become aggressive
urgency.meaning: emotional pressure is used to bypass controls — follow procedure.
